tour.title: Project Overview
tour.description: Unifolio is a mutual fund portfolio tracking and wealth-management platform for the Indian market, built as a free-core alternative to Mprofit. The README itself is just a placeholder title, but CLAUDE.md is the real map: it defines the MVP scope (CAS import, phone+OTP onboarding, a main holdings dashboard, and an analytics dashboard now under active build), the non-negotiables (Decimal everywhere for money, no raw CAS PDF or PAN storage, test-driven development), and points to the full spec set in /Docs. Every step in this tour traces back to a decision already made in those documents.

tour.title: Backend Entry Point
tour.description: backend/app/main.py is where the FastAPI application comes to life: it builds the app instance, configures CORS so the Vite dev server can talk to it, and wires in the routers for each logical service. This single file is the backbone that ties Auth, Import, Dashboard, and Analytics together into one monolith deployment, exactly as the architecture-at-a-glance in CLAUDE.md describes — one FastAPI app, four logical services, not four deployments.

tour.title: The API Surface
tour.description: These four routers are what main.py mounts, and together they define every HTTP endpoint the frontend can call. auth.py handles phone+OTP login and session refresh, imports.py exposes the two-step CAS parse/confirm flow, dashboard.py is by far the largest surface (household-member CRUD plus every per-member and family-aggregate view), and analytics.py — once a bare placeholder router — now exposes the first real Phase 4 endpoints: per-member and household-aggregate SEBI-category/AMC allocation. Seeing all four together shows the project's real shape: three services fully implemented, and a fourth now growing its first feature.

tour.title: Core Data Model
tour.description: Every service you'll see from here on reads and writes these five files. db/base.py defines the single SQLAlchemy DeclarativeBase every model inherits from; models/enums.py is the central vocabulary (transaction types, plan types, import status, ARN status) referenced across the whole schema; and user.py, folio.py, and transaction.py are the highest fan-in models in the entire codebase — the User/HouseholdMember, Folio, and Transaction tables that the FIFO holdings engine and every dashboard view ultimately depend on. Understanding these five files first makes every service you read afterward make sense immediately.

tour.title: The Decimal Discipline
tour.description: CLAUDE.md calls this out as a repeated, explicit requirement: a float anywhere in the money path is a bug. decimal_utils.py is the small, cross-cutting helper that enforces it — fixed-precision quantization for units (3dp), amounts (2dp), and NAV, used by every model and service that touches money. It's a tiny file, but it's load-bearing: skip it and the FIFO engine in Step 8 would silently accumulate rounding errors.
tour.languageLesson: Python's float uses binary floating point, which cannot represent most decimal fractions exactly — 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3. The Decimal type stores numbers in base-10, making it the only safe choice for money, units, and NAV values where cumulative rounding errors would compound into real financial discrepancies.

tour.title: CAS Import Pipeline
tour.description: This is how a user's mutual fund holdings enter the system. parser.py wraps the casparser library to turn an uploaded CAS PDF into normalized investor/scheme/transaction data; enrich.py resolves each CAS scheme name to an AMFI code via mfapi.in, using exact and fuzzy matching; and service.py orchestrates the two-step parse/confirm flow that api/imports.py from Step 3 exposes, building a TTL'd in-memory preview before anything is persisted. Note the no-raw-PDF-storage rule from CLAUDE.md in action — the PDF bytes never touch disk.

tour.title: Auth & Session Security
tour.description: Phone+OTP is the entire authentication model — no passwords. otp.py handles OTP generation, hashing, issuance, and verification with attempt lockout and expiry; session.py creates and refreshes hashed-token sessions and provides get_current_session/get_current_user, which CLAUDE.md names as the app's real security boundary; and models/auth.py is where both OtpRequest and Session are persisted, storing only hashed values, never raw OTPs or tokens. Every dashboard route from Step 3 ultimately depends on get_current_user to know which household it's serving.

tour.title: The FIFO Holdings Engine
tour.description: This is the heart of the Main Dashboard. holdings.py replays each folio's transactions as purchase lots — a same-date purchase-before-redemption tiebreak keeps consumption deterministic, a bug the session log records was found and fixed during Phase 3's final review. aggregate.py fans every dashboard view out across a user's household members with placeholder-aware handling for members with no data yet, and snapshots.py backfills monthly portfolio values by replaying those same FIFO lots and pricing them with cached NAV. All three build directly on the Transaction and Folio models from Step 4, and this same engine is reused directly by the new analytics allocation service in Step 10.

tour.title: Dashboard View Services
tour.description: Beyond holdings, the dashboard exposes several derived views, each a small, focused service: allocation.py buckets current holdings into asset classes and AMCs for the Main Dashboard; sip.py detects an active SIP by checking for a recent PURCHASE_SIP transaction; cash_flow.py builds a chronological ledger of debits and credits, excluding internal switch transfers; distributor_comparison.py (PRD-03 FR-11) groups a scheme's folios by distributor ARN and reruns the FIFO engine per group; and nav.py is the on-demand NAV cache standing in for a future scheduled job, degrading gracefully to stale cache on outage. Each one reads the same holdings data from Step 8 through a different lens.

tour.title: Analytics: Category & AMC Allocation
tour.description: This is the first slice of the standalone Analytics dashboard (PRD-04, Phase 4 Part 1), built deliberately by reusing rather than duplicating what already exists: services/analytics/allocation.py calls into the same FIFO holdings engine from Step 8, batch-fetches each scheme's SEBI category, and aggregates current value into percentage-weighted SEBI-category and AMC buckets. schemas.py defines the Pydantic response shapes pairing those buckets with per-member aggregate status, and the two new routes on api/analytics.py from Step 3 expose per-member and household-aggregate allocation views. Where Step 9's dashboard/allocation.py answers 'what does one member's portfolio look like today', this new service is the foundation for the broader cross-household analytics views still to come.

tour.title: The Database Schema
tour.description: The Database-Schema-Unifolio.md doc is the exact, final schema every model in Steps 4 and 7-9 was built against — including the reference-data-vs-user-data separation and the transactions/nav_history partitioning that CLAUDE.md insists must be preserved, not simplified away. The 0001_initial_schema.py migration is where that design actually lands: users, sessions, household_members, folios, transactions, and reference tables, created via Alembic rather than a hand-edited schema, exactly as the non-negotiables require.
tour.languageLesson: Alembic migrations are versioned, ordered Python scripts with upgrade()/downgrade() functions. Each migration captures one incremental schema change, so the database can evolve in lockstep with the ORM models instead of drifting out of sync with hand-edited DDL.

tour.title: Frontend Entry Point
tour.description: frontend/src/main.tsx is the React equivalent of Step 2's main.py: it mounts the root App component into the DOM inside React StrictMode. apiClient.ts is the shared foundation every feature module builds on — the base API URL constant and an ApiError class used across the whole SPA, so every backend router from Step 3 has exactly one corresponding client-side entry point for constructing requests.

tour.title: Frontend Auth & Onboarding
tour.description: This is the highest fan-in cluster on the frontend. api.ts wraps every OTP-login and household-member-CRUD fetch call, attaching the bearer token from session storage — the client-side mirror of Step 7's session.py. AuthContext.tsx resumes a session from the stored token on mount, and OnboardingFlow.tsx plus FamilyImportFlow.tsx are the two big orchestrators built on top of it: a back-navigable questionnaire history stack, and the sequential per-member CAS upload queue that ultimately calls into Step 6's import pipeline.

tour.title: Frontend Dashboard UI
tour.description: DashboardView.tsx is the main dashboard screen — it fetches holdings and allocation for either the family aggregate or a single household member, the same family/per-member duality that Step 8's aggregate.py implements on the backend. dashboard/api.ts is its dedicated client: a shared authFetch wrapper with typed getters for all eleven member-scoped and family-aggregate dashboard routes exposed back in Step 3. Together these close the loop from database row to rendered screen, and the analytics feature from Step 10 is the next surface waiting for a frontend home of its own.

tour.title: Infrastructure & CI/CD
tour.description: docker-compose.yml defines the local Postgres 16 container used for functional-test parity with production, per the SQLite-to-Postgres migration plan referenced in CLAUDE.md — local development stays on SQLite, but this container lets tests run against real Postgres before anything touches AWS. ci.yml is the capstone: it runs the fast SQLite pytest suite, a separate Postgres-functional suite against that same container, and the frontend build/test pipeline on every push and pull request, enforcing the test-driven, always non-negotiable across the whole monorepo — including the new analytics allocation tests introduced alongside Step 10.
tour.languageLesson: docker-compose service definitions declare desired container state — image, ports, volumes, health checks — so the same Postgres version used in CI matches what a developer runs locally, eliminating 'works on my machine' schema drift.
